problem_evidence.fact: FDA observed 397 retail deli departments in 2015-2016: 70.0% were out of compliance on 'foods requiring refrigeration are held at proper temperature' (data item 5), 62.9% on 'foods are cooled properly' (data item 7), and the improper holding/time-and-temperature risk factor as a whole was out of compliance in 91.2% of delis.

FDA's 10-year trend study (roughly 850 establishments observed per data-collection phase across nine facility types) found that in 2008 only 45% of full-service restaurants and 49% of delis were 'in compliance' with the improper holding (time and temperature) risk factor - i.e. a majority were not.

New Jersey defines 'refrigeration temperatures' as 41 F or less (a 45 F allowance applied only to equipment in use before Jan 2, 2007 that had to be upgraded or replaced by Jan 2, 2012), and requires potentially hazardous food to be held at refrigeration temperatures except during prep/cooking/cooling or approved time-as-control.

NJ's cooling rule is two-stage and the stages are cumulative, not concurrent: N.J.A.C. 8:24-3.5(d)1 reads 'i. Within two hours, from 135 degrees Fahrenheit to 70 degrees Fahrenheit; and ii. Within four hours, from 70 degrees Fahrenheit to refrigeration temperatures.' The four-hour clock starts at 70 F, so the total allowed window is up to six hours, not four - a rule that can only be evidenced with timestamped readings.

avenues.established_pattern: Three independent signals per refrigerated unit, not one: (1) product-simulating temperature probe (probe in a glycol bottle or a buffered simulant, not just air temperature, because air temp swings on every door open and every defrost cycle), (2) magnetic reed/door contact to catch a door left ajar and to suppress nuisance alarms during stocking, (3) power/compressor state from a current clamp or a gateway on a UPS, so a power loss is reported even when the sensor itself is dead. Gateway publishes to MQTT, a local database keeps the immutable series, and a rules engine fires on persistence (e.g. product temp >41 F for >30 min) plus degree-minutes accumulation, with escalation tiers. The same rules engine must model NJ's cooling curve as two sequential deadlines - 135 F to 70 F inside 2 hours, then 70 F to refrigeration temperature inside 4 further hours (up to 6 hours total) per ...
avenues.fine_tuning_needed: No, for the core product. Temperature thresholds, the two-stage cooling deadlines from N.J.A.C. 8:24-3.5(d)1, degree-minute accumulation and door-ajar persistence are deterministic rules, and a 450M-2B VLM reads a seven-segment cooler display or a dial thermometer zero-shot well enough for triage. Fine-tuning only becomes worth it if we sell camera-based product-state classification (is that pan of sliced turkey in the case or on the prep table) - that needs a few hundred labeled frames per ...

avenues.established_pattern: IP cameras -> local NVR running a person/object detector plus multi-object tracker -> zone and line-crossing rules per camera (each SCO lane, the bagging area, back door inside/outside, receiving dock, cash-wrap till) -> fusion with transaction events (POS export or SCO scan events) -> exception scoring and de-duplication -> short clip + still queued for human review -> reviewer confirms or rejects, and rejections feed back as training negatives. A small vision-language model is used only as a second stage on flagged clips (describe what is in the basket or hands, read a receipt or label), never as the primary alarm. This mirrors how published systems work: detection plus tracking to get stable person/object tracks, then a separate classifier over the track's trajectory or the POS-video comparison for lane-level events.
avenues.fine_tuning_needed: Split answer. Zone, loitering, back-door and receiving rules need no fine-tuning - a stock person detector plus zones is enough, and Frigate will run either its bundled models or a custom model with its own label map. Item-level scan-bagging detection does need a custom detector trained on that store's own camera angles and packaging, plus per-store threshold calibration against a labelled week of footage; there is no off-the-shelf model that knows 'this box of cereal moved from hand to bag ...

Practical rule for a shelf system: buy cameras with microphones disabled or absent, and never record audio.

public: Google/Yelp reviews that mention specific empty shelves, 'couldn't find', or a price that rang up higher than the tag (a recurring phrase pattern is the strongest low-cost signal). (inference)
Weekly circular size and page count — more advertised items means more tag changes per week and more chances for a mismatch. (inference)
Store footprint and aisle count published on the store's own site or in a shopping-center lease flyer; 8+ aisles with 15+ staff is where a walk stops happening. (inference)
Number of locations (1–10 is the sweet spot; above that they are already talking to Simbe/Focal). (inference)

Co-op/wholesaler affiliation visible on signage or the site (Wakefern/ShopRite, Key Food, IGA, Associated) — Wakefern members may already get shelf tools through the co-op (Simbe's Tally is deployed at two Wakefern members), so prioritize ...
Job postings for 'price integrity', 'planogram', 'reset crew' or overnight stocker roles — evidence that tag/shelf labor is a named, unfilled job. (inference)
NJ Division of Consumer Affairs / OAG press releases and OWM enforcement actions naming a banner (public, but only large chains appear).
Store photos on Google Maps that show empty facings, handwritten price signs or cases sitting in the aisle. (inference)
walk_in: Holes with no shelf tag versus holes with a tag — the first is a stocking gap, the second is a planogram/price gap; count both per aisle for 10 minutes.
Handwritten, taped or expired promo signs; tag facings that don't match the product in front of them.
Overstock on top stock or cut cases parked in the aisle (a sign the store restocks from the back by memory, not by list). (inference)
Number of staff on the floor at 2–4 pm and whether anyone carries a handheld scanner or a printed pick list.
Existing camera domes: count them, check whether they are IP/ONVIF (label on the housing) and whether any point at shelves rather than the door.
Register/POS model and receipt format — can you get an item-level sales export, or is the only data a Z-report? (inference)
Paper shelf tags versus electronic shelf labels; ESLs mean the price half of the pitch is already solved and only availability remains. (inference)
Backroom: is there a labeled location for each overstock item, or is it floor-stacked? (inference)

pilot.scope: One store, 2–4 weeks. Week 1: baseline — two manual gap/price audits per day for five days on a fixed 10–15 aisle route, plus a POS item-level export. Week 2: install 4 fixed PoE cameras on the highest-velocity aisles, build the realogram from captured images, label 300–500 shelf images, fine-tune the detector. Weeks 3–4: daily operation — one 5-minute phone walk per shift plus continuous fixed-camera monitoring on priority aisles, alerts pushed to the store's existing task channel, weekly ...
pilot.hardware: 4x 4K PoE cameras (page-1 prices $80–$200 list / $48–$120 current each), PoE switch, one Jetson Orin Nano Super ($249, supports up to four cameras so this is the ceiling for a single Jetson) or an Intel mini-PC as the local inference box, existing staff phone for the walk, cart/phone mount, cabling. Everything on-prem; no cloud dependency, no audio capture.
pilot.success_metric: Primary: at least 25% fewer empty facings on the audited route at the 2 pm audit versus baseline. Secondary: ≥90% of gap alerts confirmed real by staff (precision), price-tag mismatch count reduced by half, and ≤10 minutes/day of added staff time. (thresholds are targets, not findings)
pilot.cost_range: $4,500–$9,500 for the pilot: cameras plus Jetson $440–$730 at the prices cited above, plus an unsourced allowance for switch, cabling, mounts and labor (assume $700–$1,600 all-in hardware), 35–55 hours of build/install/labeling at $100–$125/hr ($3,500–$6,900), plus travel. Ongoing service after the pilot: $300–$700/month per store. Assumes one store, 10–15 aisles, existing Wi-Fi or a $150–$300 cabling run, client supplies POS export, and no custom hardware enclosure.
pilot.assumptions: Assumes the store will give a POS export (CSV or API) and 30 minutes of staff time on day one; assumes an 8–15k sq ft sales floor with 2.1–2.4 m shelving; excludes electronic shelf labels, excludes any customer analytics, and assumes the detector fine-tune reaches roughly 80–86% AP on the store's own images — the low end of what the Croatian study reports, because US packaging and lighting differ (inference). If labeling needs exceed 800 images, add 15–25 hours.

risks: Independents may not pay a recurring fee for a problem they have tolerated for years; the value story has to be price-accuracy penalty avoidance and night-crew hours, not 'AI'.
Most independents have no accurate planogram (Simbe says as much), so the installer absorbs the cost of building a realogram — unbilled hours in the first store of every account.
False positives erode trust fast; if staff chase 10 bad alerts they stop using the list within a week.

Fixed cameras are a poor fit for full-store coverage (a few feet of shelf per camera, and a single Jetson Orin Nano Super accepts up to four cameras), so the phone walk is load-bearing and depends on staff compliance.
